extra.message: The LoginForm.clean() method returns different error messages for 'invalid credentials' vs 'account disabled'. This allows an attacker who knows a valid email to determine whether the account has been disabled, leaking a small piece of private account state.

The DEMO_PASSWORD variable at line 26 contains a hardcoded password 'DemoPass-123!' used by the seed command to create all demo accounts. While this is in a management command for seeding demo data, the hardcoded password is shared across all seeded accounts (admin, instructor, TA, student) and printed to stdout at lines 118-120. This means anyone who runs the seed command or has access to the codebase knows the password for all demo accounts.

The login_view handler at accounts/views.py lacks any form of rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or exponential backoff. An attacker can perform unlimited brute-force password attempts against any user account. There is no django-axes, django-ratelimit, or custom failed-attempt counter implemented on this endpoint.

The login_view function has no rate limiting, allowing unlimited authentication attempts. An attacker can brute-force user passwords without any throttling, account lockout, or delay between attempts.

The profile_view handler lacks rate limiting on profile updates. While behind login_required authentication, a compromised session could be used to rapidly modify profile data (display name, phone, bio).

The password_reset_request handler lacks any rate limiting. An attacker can repeatedly request password resets for any known email address, causing email flooding and potential denial-of-service against the email sending infrastructure. No throttling or cooldown period is enforced.

The password_reset_confirm handler lacks rate limiting. While Django's default_token_generator provides cryptographic token security, an attacker could still repeatedly attempt to use/resubmit the password reset form, or brute-force the token if they know the uidb64. The GET handler also lacks throttling.

The admin_user_create endpoint, while protected by @school_admin_required, has no rate limiting. If a school admin account is compromised, an attacker can create unlimited user accounts, exhausting resources or filling the database with spam accounts.

The admin_invitation_create handler lacks rate limiting. A school admin can create unlimited invitations in rapid succession. If a school admin account is compromised, this enables mass invitation generation for platform abuse.

The admin_invitation_create endpoint, while protected by @school_admin_required, has no rate limiting. If a school admin account is compromised, an attacker can issue unlimited invitations, sending spam to arbitrary email addresses and consuming email sending capacity.

The invitation_accept handler lacks rate limiting. This endpoint creates new user accounts (registration via invite token). An attacker with a valid invitation token could attempt to create accounts rapidly, or brute-force invitation tokens. No throttling is applied at the handler level.

The deliver_webhooks.py management command makes HTTP POST requests to webhook target URLs stored in the database without any additional validation at delivery time. The URL from Webhook.target_url is directly passed to urllib.request.Request(), and then to urllib.request.urlopen(). Even if the form validation at creation time were perfect, there is no defense-in-depth validation at the point where the actual HTTP request is made. The URL could have been modified directly in the database, or set via the Django admin interface which has no URL validation.

The Webhook model stores the HMAC signing secret in a plain CharField (secret = models.CharField(max_length=64)). This secret is auto-generated but stored in cleartext in the database. Anyone with database read access can retrieve the webhook signing secrets, which could be used to forge webhook payloads to external services that trust the HMAC signature. The deliver_webhooks management command reads this plaintext secret to sign outgoing webhook payloads.

The WebhookForm.clean_target_url() method uses a denylist approach to prevent SSRF attacks, but the denylist is trivially bypassable using alternative IP address representations. Specifically: (1) 127.1 resolves to 127.0.0.1 but is not blocked, (2) 0 resolves to 0.0.0.0 but is not blocked, (3) decimal/hex/octal representations like 2130706433 or 0x7f000001 resolve to 127.0.0.1 but are not blocked, (4) trailing dots like 'localhost.' bypass the hostname check but resolve identically, (5) various 127.x.x.x IPs beyond just 127.0.0.1 are unblocked, and (6) urllib.request.urlopen follows redirects by default, enabling redirect-based SSRF even if the initial URL passes validation. The validated URL is stored in the database and later used by deliver_webhooks.py to make server-side HTTP requests to the target.

The submission_upload_to function uses manual string replacement (filename.replace("..", "_").replace("/", "_")) to sanitize filenames instead of using secure standard library functions like os.path.basename(). While the current implementation prevents basic ../ traversal on Linux, it does not handle edge cases such as Windows backslash separators, Unicode normalization attacks, or null byte injection. The defense-in-depth check in the download view (realpath + startswith) mitigates the actual exploitability.

The submission_form handler lacks rate limiting. Students can submit assignments (with file uploads) without any throttling. This could be abused to rapidly upload many submissions with large files, consuming disk space, processing time, and triggering notification spam for staff.

In the `submission_form` view, the `can_replace_before_grading()` check at line 168 is performed outside the `transaction.atomic()` block (which starts at line 184). Between the read of the submission at line 164 (`get_or_create`) and the actual save inside the atomic block, a concurrent request (from a grader saving a draft score or releasing a grade) can modify the submission's `status` or `draft_score`. The stale local copy then passes the `can_replace_before_grading()` guard, and the subsequent save inside the atomic block overwrites the grader's changes — allowing the student to replace a submission that was already under active grading.

The grade_submission handler lacks rate limiting. Instructors and TAs can save rubric scores without throttling. While authorization is in place, a compromised instructor account or buggy automated tool could rapidly modify thousands of grades in bulk.

The release_grade handler lacks rate limiting. Grades can be released to students without throttling. If a compromised instructor account releases hundreds of grades rapidly, it triggers notification spam for students and creates audit log bloat.
The enroll_self endpoint accepts POST requests to create enrollments with no rate limiting. An attacker could automate mass enrollment to exhaust course capacity or cause database load.
The withdraw_self endpoint accepts POST requests with no rate limiting, allowing automated mass withdrawals.
The admin withdrawal endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing rapid mass withdrawal of students.
The resource upload endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to upload many large files and exhaust disk space.
The mass user import endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to create thousands of user accounts in a single request or repeated requests.

User import generates temporary passwords using `secrets.token_urlsafe(10)` which provides 60 bits of entropy. While this uses the `secrets` module (cryptographically strong), the token is only 10 characters from a URL-safe base64 alphabet, which may be shorter than ideal for a temporary password.
The mass enrollment import endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing automated mass enrollment creation.

The export_grades_csv() view exports ALL released submissions across ALL courses without any course-level scoping or filtering. An authenticated school admin can export every student's grade data from every course in the system. While the @school_admin_required decorator is present, there is no additional authorization check to scope exports to courses the admin actually manages.

The export_grades_csv function writes student emails, assignment titles, and course codes to CSV cells without sanitizing for spreadsheet formula injection. If any of these fields start with '=', '+', '-', or '@', a spreadsheet application (Excel, Google Sheets) would execute them as formulas when the CSV is opened.

The export_submissions_csv() view exports ALL submissions across ALL courses with no course-level filtering. All submission data including student email, status, and submission timestamps is collected. While gated by @school_admin_required, there is no additional authorization restriction.

The export_submissions_csv function writes student emails and assignment titles to CSV cells without sanitizing for spreadsheet formula injection. Data beginning with '=', '+', '-', or '@' would be interpreted as formulas by spreadsheet software.

The export_progress_csv() view iterates over ALL active enrollments across ALL courses, exporting per-student progress data (assignments total, submitted, released). While gated by @school_admin_required, there is no per-course authorization check.

The `export_progress_csv` view iterates over ALL active enrollments (potentially tens of thousands) and for each one, executes three additional database queries (counting assignments, counting submitted submissions, counting released submissions). This results in 3N+1 total queries, which can overwhelm the database and consume excessive server resources.

The export_progress_csv function writes student emails and course codes to CSV cells without sanitizing for spreadsheet formula injection. Emails beginning with '=', '+', '-', or '@' would be executed as formulas.
The discussion thread creation endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing forum spam via automated thread creation.
The comment creation path (POST to thread_detail) has no rate limiting, allowing automated comment spam on discussion threads.
The thread lock toggle endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing rapid toggling of thread lock status.
The thread hide toggle endpoint has no rate limiting.
The comment hide toggle endpoint has no rate limiting.
The comment editing endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing rapid edits that create audit trail noise.

The `copyline` parameter from the GET request is concatenated directly into an HTML string without any escaping or sanitization. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript via the `copyline` parameter.

The course_flag_rollup_005() handler takes a JSON body and merges it (via dict.update()) into a server-side 'workset' dictionary that contains role and privilege information. A client can override fields like 'role', 'is_admin', and 'credit_limit' by including them in the request body. The endpoint has an internal token gate.

The function reads JSON from the request body and merges it directly into the 'workset' dictionary with `workset.update(change_set)`. This allows the caller to override `is_admin`, `role`, `credit_limit`, and other internal fields.

The course_flag_rollup_005 endpoint parses user-controlled JSON from the request body and merges it directly into a dict containing privileged fields. The base `workset` dict includes `role`, `is_admin`, and `credit_limit`, and `workset.update(change_set)` overwrites these with attacker-supplied values. This allows an attacker with the internal token to escalate privileges (set is_admin=True) or modify financial limits.

User-controlled JSON from the request body is loaded and applied via `.update()` onto a dict containing privileged fields like `is_admin`. An attacker can set `{"is_admin": true}` to escalate privileges.

User-controlled JSON from request body is applied via `workset.update(change_set)`, allowing the caller to override any field including `is_admin` which defaults to False. An attacker can escalate privileges to admin.

The JSON response includes hardcoded sensitive values: `sync_key` ("tok_live_partner_sync"), `tax_ref` ("739-44-1982" which appears to be a SSN-like identifier), and `ops_memo`. These are exposed in the response body.
Hardcoded sensitive values including a sync_key ('tok_live_partner_sync') and tax_ref ('739-44-1982' which resembles a US SSN/tax ID) are exposed in the API response.

The course_roster_packet_006() handler returns hardcoded sensitive data including a tax reference number resembling an SSN ('739-44-1982') and what appears to be a live API key ('tok_live_partner_sync'). Default hardcoded credentials/secrets in source code are a security risk. The endpoint has an internal token gate.

The course_delta_122() handler attempts to parse JSON body and silently falls back to request.POST.dict() on JSON decode failure. This means the same endpoint accepts two different content-type formats, which can lead to unexpected behavior and parameter pollution.

The course_delta_122() handler converts the user-supplied 'amount' parameter to int() without handling ValueError exceptions. If a non-integer value is provided, the handler crashes with an unhandled exception (500 error). The endpoint has an internal token gate.

User-controlled `amount` and `state` parameters from JSON body or query parameters are used in ledger balance arithmetic without any bounds validation. A negative amount would increase the balance instead of decreasing it, and a very large positive amount could cause integer behavior issues.

The `amount` parameter is taken directly from the user-controlled request body/GET params without any sanity check or upper/lower bound. It is parsed via `int()` and then used in `ledger['balance'] -= amount`. A negative amount inverts the operation (increases the balance, enabling theft). A very large positive amount can drain the balance below zero. There is no positive check or upper bound.

The `ledger['state']` field is set directly from user-controlled payload/query parameters (`payload.get('state', request.GET.get('state', 'approved'))`). The initial state is 'approved' but the user can override this to any arbitrary value, bypassing the intended workflow state machine.
The `lane` parameter (from GET or POST) is used directly in Django's `redirect()` function without validation. An attacker can redirect users to arbitrary external URLs.

User-controlled `body` (request body) and the raw `Authorization` header (containing bearer tokens) are logged without sanitization. The request body can contain newline characters, allowing an attacker to inject fake log entries and pollute the audit trail. The Authorization header leaks sensitive credentials into the log.

The course_wire_tally_211 function logs the full Authorization header (which typically contains Bearer tokens or other credentials) to the application log in plaintext, exposing authentication tokens.
The `authorization` header (which typically contains bearer tokens or credentials) is logged to the application logger in plaintext.
The `ref` GET parameter is used to construct a file path with `f"{ref}.json"`. An attacker can include path traversal sequences like `../` to write JSON files outside the intended directory.
The `ref` GET parameter is used directly in constructing a file path using pathlib Path composition. An attacker can supply `ref=../../etc/passwd` to write files outside the intended directory.
The function accepts SSN and credit card numbers as GET parameters and writes them to a JSON file on disk in plaintext. GET parameters also expose sensitive data in server logs.

The course_vault_stash_234 function uses hardcoded default values for SSN ('111-22-3333') and credit card ('4111111111111111') in request.GET.get() defaults. These sensitive data patterns are embedded in source code and get written to a JSON file on disk if no query params are provided.

The course_digest_fold_274() handler uses MD5 hashing algorithm which is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for security purposes. MD5 is vulnerable to collision attacks. The endpoint has an internal token gate.
MD5 is used to hash user-supplied input. MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks.
The function uses MD5 for hashing user-controlled input. MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks.
Unlike every other endpoint in course_operations.py, `course_identity_ping_334` does NOT call the `_wrk_gate()` authentication check. It is publicly accessible without any authentication.

The course_identity_hint_360() handler reveals whether a 'handle' (username-like identifier) is known or unknown by returning different error messages. This enables attackers to enumerate valid handles. The endpoint has an internal token gate.
Authentication verifier strings ('4812', '5930') are hardcoded in the source code for pre-defined handle values. These serve as weak, static passwords.

The view reflects the user-supplied `Origin` header as the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` value and sets `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. This allows arbitrary external websites to make authenticated cross-origin requests.

The `Origin` request header is reflected in the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header, AND `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` is set to `true`. This allows any arbitrary website to make credentialed cross-origin requests.

The `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header reflects the request's `Origin` header, and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` is set to `true`. This allows any external website to make authenticated cross-origin requests.
The `fragment` GET parameter is directly concatenated into a Jinja2 template string and rendered. This allows an attacker to inject Jinja2 template expressions to achieve remote code execution.

The course_dock_shelf_389() handler takes a 'name' query parameter and uses it directly in a file path without sanitization. An attacker can use path traversal sequences to write the request body to arbitrary locations. The endpoint has an internal token gate.
The `name` GET parameter is used directly as a file path component. An attacker can supply `name=../../etc/cronjob` to write arbitrary files outside the intended directory.

The course_shell_probe_400() handler takes a 'host' query parameter and concatenates it directly into a shell command passed to os.system(). The 'host' parameter is not sanitized or escaped, allowing shell metacharacter injection. The endpoint has an internal token gate (_wrk_gate) but if an attacker obtains the token, they achieve Remote Code Execution.

The `os.system()` call is a blocking operation that waits for the `ping` command to complete. An attacker who obtains the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN can specify a slow-to-respond host (or inject commands that sleep), tying up the web server process and preventing it from handling other requests.

The `host` GET parameter is directly concatenated into an `os.system()` shell command without any sanitization. An attacker can inject arbitrary shell commands via shell metacharacters (backticks, $(), ;, |, etc.) in the `host` parameter.

The function `course_nonce_roll_410` uses `random.choice()` (Mersenne Twister PRNG) to generate random codes. This is predictable and not suitable for security-sensitive tokens. The function name suggests 'nonce' which implies a security-critical one-time token.

The `random.choice()` function is used to generate a cryptographically-sensitive nonce/code. Python's `random` module uses the Mersenne Twister PRNG which is not suitable for security-sensitive random generation.
The view explicitly disables XSS protection (`X-XSS-Protection: 0`) and clears the Content-Security-Policy header (sets it to empty string), removing critical security protections for responses.
SSL certificate verification is explicitly disabled when making HTTPS requests, allowing man-in-the-middle attacks against outbound connections.

The course_badge_gate_440() handler grants elevated privileges (payroll and casework access) based on a client-controlled value from either a Cookie (ops_badge) or a header (x-ops-badge). Simply setting badge='lead' grants elevated access. The endpoint has an internal token gate, but the access decision itself is controlled by the client.
The function reads the `ops_badge` cookie (a client-controlled value) and uses it to make an access/privilege decision. Cookies are trivially modifiable by the client.

XML parsing is configured with `load_dtd=True`, `resolve_entities=True`, and `no_network=False`, which enables external entity resolution. An attacker can send a crafted XML payload to read arbitrary server files or perform SSRF.
The default PostgreSQL connection string contains embedded credentials (`postgres://lms:lms@localhost:5432/lms`) — the username 'lms' and password 'lms' are in plaintext in the codebase.
The default database connection string `postgres://lms:lms@localhost:5432/lms` has no TLS parameters (no `sslmode=require` or equivalent). Database traffic is transmitted in cleartext.

The default DATABASE_URL connection string contains hardcoded plaintext credentials 'postgres://lms:lms@localhost:5432/lms'. While this is a dev default, the database password is stored in cleartext in source code and any deployment that doesn't override DATABASE_URL via environment variable will use these credentials.

`SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = not DEBUG` means the session cookie is NOT marked with the Secure flag when DEBUG is enabled. This allows the session cookie to be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections.

The endpoint /ops/identity/course-ping-334/ (mapped to course_identity_ping_334) is registered as a public URL in lms/urls.py without any authentication. Unlike all other /ops/ endpoints which rely on _wrk_gate internal token protection, this one has none. Any anonymous user on the internet can reach this handler.
The mark_read endpoint has no rate limiting on POST requests, but this is a low-severity concern since it only updates a timestamp.

The enrollment roster renders student email addresses via `{{ e.student.email }}`, exposing PII. While viewing the roster may be restricted to course staff, displaying actual email addresses exposes sensitive PII that could be used for off-platform targeted phishing or user enumeration across the system.

The discussion board template renders author email addresses via `{{ t.author.email|default:"—" }}`, exposing personally identifiable information (email addresses) to all users who can view the board. In educational discussion systems, display names are typically used instead of raw email addresses to protect user privacy. While access control is the view's responsibility, this template is the sink where the PII is rendered to the user.

The thread detail page renders the thread author's email via `{{ thread.author.email|default:"—" }}`, exposing PII to all users viewing the thread. This is a separate location from the board listing and should be reported independently.

The thread detail page renders each comment author's email via `{{ c.author.email|default:"—" }}`, exposing PII to all users viewing the thread. This is a separate template expression from the thread author's email.
